title: Truck Tour
directAnswer: A unique valid start exists when total petrol ≥ total distance. Find it in one pass: track a running tank from a candidate start; the moment it goes negative at pump i, no start in [candidate..i] can work, so jump the candidate to i+1 and reset the tank. The last surviving candidate is the answer — O(n) time, O(1) space.

remember.pattern: Greedy single pass: reset start when running balance dips below zero
remember.formula:
total = 0; tank = 0; start = 0
for i in range(n):
    diff = petrol[i] - distance[i]
    total += diff
    tank += diff
    if tank < 0:
        start = i + 1
        tank = 0
return start   # guaranteed valid since total >= 0
rules: If `tank` (running balance from the current candidate) drops below 0 at pump `i`, **no** pump in `[start..i]` is a valid start — move `start = i + 1` and reset `tank = 0`.
Keep a separate `total` over all pumps; the tour is feasible iff `total ≥ 0`, and then the found start is the unique answer.
`diff = petrol[i] − distance[i]` is the net fuel gained crossing pump i to the next.
Reset only the local `tank`, never `total` — total verifies global feasibility.
Single pass, no need to simulate the wrap-around explicitly once you know total ≥ 0.
whenToUse: Circular route 'where can I start to complete the loop?' (gas station) problems

remember.takeaway: The gas-station insight: if you run out of fuel reaching pump i from start s, then every pump between s and i is also a doomed start, so skip straight to i+1. One pass finds the unique start whenever total petrol ≥ total distance.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you find the O(n) greedy instead of trying every start (O(n²)), and can justify why a failing prefix lets you skip all starts within it.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Trying every starting pump with a full simulation (O(n²) → TLE), or resetting the global total when the local tank goes negative.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Prove the skip lemma (if start s fails at i, no s..i works), state the total ≥ 0 feasibility condition, and note this is the same prefix-reset logic as Kadane and Gas Station.

problemStatement:
A truck must complete a circular tour of `n` petrol pumps. Pump `i` gives `petrol[i]` units of fuel, and the distance from pump `i` to the next pump (pump `(i+1) mod n`) costs `distance[i]` units of fuel (1 unit per km). The truck has an unlimited tank and starts empty.

Find the **index of the first petrol pump** from which the truck can start and complete the full circular tour, returning to the start. It is guaranteed that a unique solution exists.
constraints: A valid starting pump is guaranteed to exist (total petrol ≥ total distance)
An O(n²) simulation times out — aim for O(n)
understanding: Crossing from pump i to the next nets `petrol[i] − distance[i]` fuel. A start is valid if, beginning there with an empty tank and going around the circle, the running fuel never dips below zero. Because a valid start is guaranteed, the only question is *which* index — and a single greedy pass finds it.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is a valid start guaranteed, or must I detect impossibility?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: This problem guarantees one exists (total petrol ≥ total distance). The general Gas Station variant returns −1 when total < 0.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the route circular?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — after the last pump you return toward pump 0. The greedy avoids explicit wrap simulation because total ≥ 0 certifies the wrap closes.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can there be more than one valid start?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The problem states a unique solution. The greedy returns that single start.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What does negative running fuel mean?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The truck ran out before reaching a pump — that candidate start (and everything from it up to the failure point) is invalid.

From pump 0: 4, 3, 2, 4 — never negative. Start 0 works.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Simulate From Every Start
approaches.whenToMention: Mention to frame the problem and the feasibility check, then note O(n²) times out at n = 10⁵.
hints: The definition is direct: try each pump as the start and simulate the whole loop, checking the tank never goes negative.
For start s, walk all n pumps in circular order accumulating petrol − distance; if it stays ≥ 0 the whole way, s is the answer.
Each start costs O(n) to simulate and there are n starts → O(n²). For n = 10⁵ that's 10¹⁰ — too slow.
approaches.complexityReasoning: n candidate starts, each requiring an O(n) circular simulation → O(n²) time. Only a few counters → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Try every pump as a potential start. For candidate `s`, simulate the circular tour: set the tank to 0 and, for each of the `n` steps, add `petrol[(s+j) mod n] − distance[(s+j) mod n]`. If the tank ever goes negative, `s` fails; if it survives all `n` steps, `s` is the answer.

**Why it's the natural first attempt.** It's the literal definition of 'valid start'. No insight needed — just simulate each candidate fully.

**Why it's too slow.** Each simulation is O(n) and there are n candidates, giving O(n²). At n = 10⁵ that's ~10¹⁰ operations and a guaranteed timeout. The brute force is valuable only as a correctness oracle for the greedy on small inputs.
approaches.insight: Brute force re-simulates overlapping prefixes from scratch. The greedy's leap is realising that a prefix which fails at pump i rules out *every* start within it at once — so we never need to retry those.

approaches.name: Greedy Single Pass (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended solution. Lead with the skip lemma and the total ≥ 0 feasibility guarantee.
hints: Suppose starting at s you run dry reaching pump i. Could any pump strictly between s and i be a better start?
No — each of those pumps was reached with a non-negative tank from s, so starting there gives even less fuel and also fails by i. So jump the candidate start to i+1.
Track a global total of (petrol − distance). If total ≥ 0 a start exists, and the candidate left standing after one pass is it.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single sweep over n pumps with constant work each → O(n) time. A handful of counters → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Walk the pumps once, maintaining two running sums: a global `total` of net fuel across all pumps, and a local `tank` measuring net fuel since the current candidate start.

**The reset rule.** At pump `i`, add `diff = petrol[i] − distance[i]` to both. If `tank` becomes negative, the truck couldn't reach pump `i+1` starting from the current candidate. Set `start = i + 1` and reset `tank = 0`.

**Why we can skip every start in the failing block (the key lemma).** Say the candidate start is `s` and the tank first goes negative at pump `i`. For any pump `m` with `s < m ≤ i`, the tank was non-negative when we arrived at `m` (otherwise we'd have reset earlier). That means the fuel accumulated from `s` to `m−1` was `≥ 0`. So starting at `m` instead of `s` gives *no more* fuel reaching pump `i` — in fact less or equal — and would also fail by `i`. Hence none of `s..i` can be a valid start, and we jump straight to `i+1`. This is what turns O(n²) into O(n): each pump is examined once and never reconsidered as part of a failed block.

**Why `total ≥ 0` certifies the answer.** `total` is the net fuel over the entire circle. If `total ≥ 0`, a valid start must exist, and a classic result guarantees the single candidate surviving the pass is it — once you can reach the end of the array from `start` without going negative, the wrap-around (the part before `start`) is covered because the deficit there is exactly offset by the surplus after `start` (their sum is `total ≥ 0`). So we don't need to simulate the wrap explicitly.

**Why reset only `tank`, not `total`.** `tank` is local to the current candidate and must restart at each new candidate. `total` measures global feasibility across all pumps and must accumulate uninterrupted.
approaches.insight: This is the same prefix-reset reasoning as Kadane's maximum-subarray: a running sum that goes negative can't help any future start, so discard it and begin fresh. Recognising 'negative prefix ⇒ reset the start' lets you collapse a quadratic search to a single linear scan.

dryRun.intro: total = global net fuel, tank = net fuel since current start. Reset start+tank when tank < 0.

code.python:
def truck_tour(self, pumps: list[list[int]]) -> int:
    n = len(pumps)
    total = 0
    tank = 0
    start = 0
    for i in range(n):
        diff = pumps[i][0] - pumps[i][1]
        total += diff
        tank += diff
        if tank < 0:
            start = i + 1
            tank = 0
    return start if total >= 0 else -1

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Resetting the global total on failure
commonMistakesDetailed.why: total tracks whether ANY start can complete the loop and must accumulate across all pumps. Resetting it when the local tank dips negative destroys the feasibility test and can return a wrong start.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
if tank < 0:
    start = i + 1
    tank = 0
    total = 0   # wrong: loses the global feasibility sum
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if tank < 0:
    start = i + 1
    tank = 0
# total keeps accumulating

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Advancing the start to i instead of i + 1
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If the tank went negative at pump i, then pump i itself cannot be a valid start (you can't even leave it with enough fuel). The next viable candidate begins at i + 1.
